beats.trigger: ## Evaluations
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The generator sharpens against that feedback while you walk away.
beats.got: A fixed scorer and a generator that improves on its own. I need to see it.

beats.trigger: Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.
beats.got: There is reading, and it builds on the last module.

beats.trigger: **Distinguish** the one-off Module 5 judge from one that runs on every output
beats.got: A list of verbs, the same format as every programme I've sat through.

beats.trigger: Can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?
beats.got: The question is fair, and it admits the mess might win.

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: A claim that the work improves without me. Unproven so far.

beats.trigger: You can stay inside one loop. You cannot stay inside all of them.
beats.got: Humans can't review everything, so you write down what good means. That is a sensible point.

beats.trigger: measured judgment, made runnable
beats.got: A checker I built earlier, saved as a file.

beats.trigger: every number traces to a file, every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.
beats.got: The checker only confirms the claims match the sources. That is useful.

beats.trigger: Groundedness protects the floor. Steering raises the ceiling.
beats.got: A second check for whether the mail is any good, not just true. Floor and ceiling is a bit slogan-like.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing.
beats.got: If the scorer is fixed and only the writer changes, an improving score is real. That is how I'd set up a test too.

beats.trigger: The eval checks the thing that matters, at the moment where the mistake would hurt, against a standard you would defend.
beats.got: A passed eval is not the goal. The standard is.

beats.trigger: A yardstick you rewrite is not a yardstick.
beats.got: A 45-minute exercise where I run it myself. That's the right format.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: One briefing, one score, and I see what it flags. Fine.

beats.trigger: Come back to a tactic tightened by a judge you did not move.
beats.got: I leave, and the agent has rewritten its own instructions three times against a fixed scorer. That wasn't possible two years ago.

beats.trigger: If the judge file moved, the exercise failed; if only `./generation-tactic.md` moved, the loop worked.
beats.got: There is a checksum I can verify myself. I don't have to believe it.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: The round-by-round trail shows what changed. The closing line is a little theatrical.

beats.trigger: PDCA at the eval layer: Plan (generation tactic), Do (generate), Check (judge), Act (rewrite tactic).
beats.got: PDCA again, the same cycle from 2009 with new labels. I was waiting for that.

beats.trigger: Take-home: put any judge in a loop that improves the thing it scores.
beats.got: The pattern is reusable with any scorer.

beats.trigger: That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: The module itself says a good score isn't the end. That is not what I expected.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: A flat score shows the limit of the checker, not that the work is finished. I've seen KPIs go green that way.

beats.trigger: A generator that grades itself passes itself.
beats.got: Nobody has checked the judge. I'd score a handful by hand and compare. That is a real, doable thing.

beats.trigger: No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.
beats.got: Models will fix fabrication on their own. Deciding what good means stays with us.

beats.trigger: The destination is not "the human disappears."
beats.got: A recap from the snake game on. The human moves up a level, which is the usual reassurance.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?
beats.got: A checklist of conditions before I let it send anything. A decent question to ask.

beats.trigger: An ungrounded mail is a trust problem. A grounded but vague or tone-deaf mail is a usefulness problem.
beats.got: This repeats the floor and ceiling slide.

beats.trigger: Variety in, selection out, memory keeps
beats.got: Generate, pick, record, said as a slogan. Nothing new.

beats.trigger: Some categories never go without a human.
beats.got: Send decisions come in levels, and some stay human. That is more honest than I expected.

beats.trigger: Two judges now sit on disk: one keeps the work grounded, one steers it toward your standard.
beats.got: I write a second check for one kind of internal mail. Concrete enough.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: The better it works, the worse I get at spotting when it fails. Frankly, the most useful sentence in the module.

beats.trigger: This check has no instrument, only a date
beats.got: Put a date in the calendar to read one output myself, the way the recipient would.

beats.trigger: Your role in the loop is to design the conditions under which the system earns more autonomy, one loop at a time.
beats.got: A summary diagram and a closing line with some programme vocabulary in it.

beats.trigger: The judge file stays untouched: that's the integrity of the loop.
beats.got: One more pass to sharpen the tactic. The judge is untouched again.

beats.trigger: If it sounds too kind, ask: *"Which rule did you claim to remove but keep under another name? Quote both lines."*
beats.got: I'm told to doubt the agent's own summary and make it quote lines. That suits me.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: Four lines. The flat-score one is the one I'd keep.

beats.trigger: Pick one call that should run through the eval loop before anyone relies on it
beats.got: Homework: five agent calls and one to run through the loop. Reasonable, but it's another list.

beats.trigger: Trust the loop you can inspect.
beats.got: Trust what I can inspect. Fine as a rule.

take_homes: Keep the scorer fixed and let only the writer change. Then an improving score means something, and a checksum on the judge file proves it.
A flat or green score tells me about the limits of the checker. Nobody has checked the checker, so I score a handful by hand against it.
The better the loop runs, the less I watch. I put a date in the calendar to read one output the way the recipient would.

monday.move: Nothing on the programme side. If I do one thing: pick one recurring internal mail my team sends, score ten of them by hand, and put my verdicts beside a judge's.
monday.who: Me, with one analyst, if the first try shows anything
monday.when: Not Monday. Later in the week, once the steering groups are out of the calendar
monday.stop_condition: If the judge and I disagree on more than a couple of the ten, or it takes more than an afternoon, I stop
monday.blocker: The calendar and my own scepticism. I haven't yet seen this on one of my own tasks.

misconception.why: The loop of a fixed judge and a rewriting generator, with a SHA I can check, is something I couldn't have built two years ago, and I can test it myself. The module also says plainly what the loop doesn't do: flat scores, an unchecked judge, the human losing the eye. That's why I don't write it off as the last three programmes. I haven't done it on my own work yet, so 'wait and see' isn't fully dead.

one_line: First module I've sat through that tells you where its own method stops. Skip the slogans and the tail end, read the bits about checking the judge and reading the output yourself.
